analysis.one_liner: Taxes executives' set-aside retirement perks when their company's worker pension fund falls below 80% funded.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Ways and Means Committee, dying without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current tax rules, companies can set aside assets in special trusts to pay executives' deferred compensation while the worker pension plan covering everyone else is underfunded. This bill would treat those executive set-aside assets as taxable income the moment the company's worker pension falls below 80% of what it owes. The idea is to stop companies from securing special retirement deals for a handful of executives while the shared pension plan that covers regular workers falls behind.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers covered by company pension plans that are less than 80% funded, because the tax penalty would push employers to shore up the shared pension before securing executive set-aside trusts. Taxpayers also gain slightly, since executives would pay income tax sooner on deferred pay that is currently untaxed until it is paid out.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers in underfunded company pension plans

how_it_helps.text: When a company's defined benefit pension plan is funded below 80% of its promised liabilities, any assets the employer sets aside to pay executives' nonqualified deferred compensation would be treated as taxable income to those executives, rather than growing untaxed.
The bill defines the trigger precisely: the 'funding target attainment percentage' — the ratio of plan assets to the present value of all pension liabilities — must be below 80% for the tax to apply.

By removing the tax advantage of securing executive pay first, the bill changes the incentive: a company that wants to protect executive deferred compensation would have to deal with the underfunded worker pension covering its regular employees.

analysis.who_pays: Executives at companies whose pension plans are less than 80% funded would pay income tax on the value of assets set aside for their deferred compensation, and those companies would lose a tax-planning tool. The bill applies only to transfers or reservations of assets after December 31, 2005, so arrangements already in place before then are not touched.
analysis.who_pays_short: Executives at companies with underfunded pensions

drawbacks.text: The 80% threshold creates a cliff: companies funded just above it face no penalty at all, so an employer can keep workers' pension barely above the line while still securing executive set-asides tax-free.
The bill only applies to assets set aside after December 31, 2005, so executives whose companies had already established these arrangements escape the rule entirely.

Taxing the set-aside assets when they are restricted — rather than when the executive is paid — could create tax bills for executives on money they have not yet received and might never receive if the company collapses, raising questions about timing and fairness that the bill does not address.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea is sound and narrow: close a loophole that lets companies favor a few executives' retirement arrangements while the pension covering ordinary workers is underfunded. The main weaknesses are scope, not design intent — the 80% cliff and the grandfathering of pre-2006 arrangements leave much of the practice untouched. Even so, the cost is borne entirely by a small group of highly compensated executives and their employers, while the benefit flows to workers whose pensions are at risk.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and sat there until the 109th Congress ended, with no hearing, no vote, and no cosponsors.

narrative.text: Rep. Mark Kennedy of Minnesota introduced the bill on March 7, 2006, during the second session of the 109th Congress.
The same day, it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which has jurisdiction over tax law; the committee took no further action on it.
Not a single House member signed on as a cosponsor.
The 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007, and the bill died in committee without ever reaching the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Executives and employers at companies with underfunded pension plans keep the ability to set aside assets for executives' deferred compensation tax-free, with no penalty tied to how poorly funded the worker pension is. Workers in those underfunded plans gain nothing.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a lone Republican with zero cosponsors of either party, so no vote ever revealed where the parties stood.

industries.industry: Executives at companies with underfunded defined benefit pension plans
industries.note: The bill would strip the tax advantage of setting aside assets for executive deferred compensation whenever the shared worker pension is funded below 80%. Their interest in keeping the practice runs directly against workers' pension security.

industries.industry: Companies maintaining defined benefit pension plans
industries.note: Well-funded plans are unaffected, but employers whose pensions fall below 80% would lose a favored compensation tool and face pressure to fund the worker plan instead. The cost is concentrated on a small set of highly compensated employees rather than spread across the workforce.
